title: The opponent's resources and seeing 6-10 plies ahead
summary: Check intermezzi, desperados and counter-sacrifices for the opponent at every node, and hold long lines in your head with accurate piece positions.

steps.md:
## What can he do?

The most common reason a calculated combination fails is an **opponent resource**: an in-between check, a desperado capture, a counter-sacrifice, a stalemate trick. At every node of your tree ask: *what are his checks, captures and threats here — including the ones that give up material?*

The defensive side of the same skill: when you are attacked, look for **your** resources first — often there is exactly one move that holds (the engine shows a huge gap between it and everything else).

**Visualisation 6-10 plies**: keep track of every piece after each move. Common errors: "ghost pieces" (a piece that already moved), forgetting that a capture opened a line, and missing backward moves.

steps.prompt: White to move. The bishop on c3 attacks b2 and the a1-rook. Only one move holds the balance (Euwe-Alekhine, World Championship 1935)
steps.explain: **22.Nxd6!** — a counter-attack: the knight hits the queen on c8 and the e4-pawn, so Black has no time to take on b2. Slower moves lose material on the long diagonal. Engine main line: 22.Nxd6 Qb8 23.Nxe4 Bf6 24.Nd2 b5 25.e4 bxc4. (Euwe-Alekhine, World Championship 1935; checked with Stockfish 19.)

steps.prompt: White to move. The queen on h5 is attacked by the g6-pawn. Only one retreat keeps the balance (Karpov-Topalov, Dos Hermanas 1994)
steps.explain: **15.Qf3!** — from f3 the queen protects the f4-bishop and watches the long diagonal; the other retreats run into ...g5 or ...Nd4 with tempo. Engine main line: 15.Qf3 d5 16.exd5 Bxd5 17.Qd3 Qe7 18.Re1 Rad8. (Karpov-Topalov, Dos Hermanas 1994; checked with Stockfish 19.)

steps.prompt: White to move. The knight on g3 gives check. Take it or move the king? (Kasparov-Short, PCA-World Championship 1993)
steps.explain: **28.hxg3!** — take the piece; the counter-play after ...Nxf3 is less dangerous than it looks, while a king move leaves the white king in a mating net. Engine main line: 28.hxg3 Nxf3 29.Bxe5 Qxg4 30.Rh2 Nxe1 31.Qxe1 Qf3+. (Kasparov-Short, PCA-World Championship 1993; checked with Stockfish 19.)

steps.md: **Visualisation exercise.** Do not move pieces. From this position (Morphy-Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard, Paris 1858) play in your head: **13.Rxd7 Rxd7 14.Rd1 Qe6 15.Bxd7+ Nxd7.** Now answer the question in the next step.

steps.question: After 13.Rxd7 Rxd7 14.Rd1 Qe6 15.Bxd7+ Nxd7 (from the previous diagram), what does White play?
steps.explain: 16.Qb8+!! Nxb8 17.Rd8# — the knight on d7 must leave to take the queen, and the rook mates on d8 supported by the g5-bishop (which covers e7).

steps.md: **Second visualisation.** Lasker-Bauer 1889: **15.Bxh7+ Kxh7 16.Qxh5+ Kg8 17.Bxg7 Kxg7 18.Qg4+ Kh7 19.Rf3 e5 20.Rh3+ Qh6 21.Rxh6+ Kxh6.** Hold the final position in your head and answer the next question.

steps.question: In the final position of that line (after 21...Kxh6), White is to move. What wins material?
choices: 22.Qh4+ forking king and bishop on e7
steps.explain: 22.Qd7! forks the bishops on b7 and e7; White wins one of them and the game. If you had to check the board, repeat this exercise tomorrow.

steps.md:
## Assignment

- **Visualization drill** (*Train → visualization*): 3 sessions at the "read 6-8 plies" level.
- **Puzzles**: 20 *defensiveMove* and 10 *intermezzo* puzzles at your rating.
- In each puzzle you fail, write down which opponent resource you missed (check, capture, intermezzo, desperado, stalemate).

sources: Dvoretsky & Yusupov, Training for the Tournament Player
